nameStory: The 'flared thread' in this spider's name comes from the distinctive funnel-shaped web it weaves, where silken threads flare outward from a narrow retreat. Meshweavers get their family name from their habit of creating dense, sheet-like webs with a distinctive mesh pattern that looks almost like a tiny fishing net stretched between vegetation.
description: The Flared Thread Meshweaver is a small, inconspicuous spider that typically measures just 3-4 millimeters in body length - about the size of a match head. These delicate spiders have pale yellowish to light brown bodies with subtle darker markings, and their legs are proportionally long and thin. They're part of the meshweaver family, known for creating distinctive sheet webs with irregular mesh patterns that catch tiny flying insects.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for small, dense sheet webs with a funnel-shaped retreat, usually spanning 2-3 inches between low vegetation. The silk feels slightly sticky and has a fine mesh texture that catches dewdrops beautifully in morning light.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small body, typically 3-4mm long - smaller than most other web-building spiders you'll encounter. The entire spider could easily sit on a pencil eraser with room to spare.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Oval, somewhat flattened abdomen with a relatively narrow cephalothorax (front body section). The overall build appears delicate and elongated compared to rounder orb weavers.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-brown to light tan coloration with subtle darker chevron or stripe patterns on the abdomen. Colors are muted and blend well with dried vegetation.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Typically stays hidden in the funnel retreat of its web, only emerging quickly to grab prey. Vibrations on the web cause the spider to retreat deeper rather than rush out aggressively.

habitat: Found in low shrubs, tall grasses, and herbaceous plants in open woodlands, meadow edges, and disturbed areas with mixed vegetation. They prefer spots with some shelter from direct sun and wind, often building webs 1-3 feet off the ground in areas with moderate moisture. Look for their webs in brushy transition zones between forest and field.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active in late spring, beginning to build their characteristic sheet webs in May. Look for fresh, perfectly formed webs in the early morning when dew makes them visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most obvious and spiders are actively hunting. Adults are mature and may be found mating or guarding egg sacs within their web retreats.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though webs may become more tattered and harder to spot. Egg sacs are typically produced and hidden in the web structure during this time.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die with first hard frost, overwintering as eggs or possibly very young spiders in protected locations among leaf litter and bark crevices.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only one confirmed sighting, this western species somehow made it all the way from the Colorado Plateau region - that's like finding a roadrunner in a Maine forest!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small sheet web spiders like dwarf sheet weavers, but the distinctive funnel-shaped retreat and mesh pattern help distinguish it. Remember: if the web looks like a tiny camping tarp with a sleeping bag attached, you've found a meshweaver.
contextualKnowledge: This species' presence in New England is so unusual that any sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups, as it represents a significant range extension from its typical western habitat.
compareHints: Since this is the only Arethyna species documented in New England, compare it to other meshweavers in the Dictyna genus, which tend to be slightly larger and have more pronounced web decorations. Flared Thread Meshweavers have simpler, cleaner sheet webs and smaller body size than most other regional meshweaver species.
